analytic.title: Concurrency Control for Real-time Database Systems with Mixed Transactions

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper proposes a real-time concurrency control protocol called Reduced Ceiling Protocol (RCP) for database systems consisting of hard and soft real-time transactions. In the RCP, the schedulability of hard realtime transactions is guaranteed b y reserving the data items for them and by eliminating the blocking time from soft real-time transactions. Different concurrency control strategies are used to resolve the data conjlicts between different combinations of hard and soft real-time transactions. We have shown the characteristics of the schedules generated from the RCP. Simulation experiments have been performed to study the performance of the RCP as compared with the optimistic concurrency control with broadcast commit (OCC-BC). It has been found that the RCP can guarantee the performance of the hard real-time transactions and at the same time reduce the number of deadline missing of the soft real-time transactions.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In recent years, the research on real-time database systems (RTDBS) has received a lot of interest 12, 8, 111. One of the major issues in the design of RTDBS is transaction scheduling whose objectives are to meet transaction deadlines and to maintain database consistency [ 11. Database consistency is maintained by the use of concurrency control protocols. However, the concurrency control protocols for conventional database systems, such as two phase locking and optimistic concurrency control (OCC) [ 3 ] , are not suitable for RTDBS as they do not consider the transaction priorities in scheduling data and in resolving data conflicts. A higher priority transaction may be blocked by a lower transaction due to data conflict. This is highly undesirable and can greatly affect the schedulability of the systems 11, 91.

In recent years, different real-time concurrency control protocols (RT-CCPs) have been proposed for different types of RTDBS. Two surveys of the proposed protocols can be found in [2, 111. These protocols are mainly for the RTDBS with single types of transactions such as transactions with the same criticality. The wellknown Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP), which is for the scheduling of tasks in hard real-time systems [6, lo], has extended for the scheduling of hard real-time transactions [9]. With the PCP, the deadlines of all the hard real-time transactions can be guaranteed for a given workload and system configuration.

Other proposed RT-CCPs are for soft and firm RTDBS 11, 4, 51. They use heuristics to resolve the data conflicts between transactions with different priorities. Their prime objective is to minimize the number of deadline missing instead to guarantee the transaction deadlines. Some of the proposals are High Priority Two Phase Locking (HP-2PL) [ 11 and real-time optimistic concurrency control (RT-OCC) [4, 51. In HP-2PL, whenever there is a lock conflict and the priority of the lock requesting transaction is higher than the lock holding transaction, the lock holding transaction will be restarted.

In the RT-OCC protocols, resolution of data conflicts is delayed until a transaction has finished all its operations. A validation test is performed to ensure that the resulting schedule is serializable if the validating transaction is allowed to commit. Otherwise, the validating transaction or the other conflicting transactions will be restarted dependent on the conflict resolution method used'. In the optimistic concurrency control with broadcast commit (OCC-BC), all the transactions, which are in conflict with the validating transactions, will be restarted.
In [4], different strategies have been proposed to determine how to select the transaction for restart.

Due to the growth of real-time database applications, there is a trend of RTDBS to integrate with other systems, which may or may not be real-time in nature [lo]. For example, in an integrated computer manufacturing system, the control systems in the production lines may integrate with the higher-level management systems. In this kind of RTDBS, it is likely to have transactions with different levels of criticality. Some of the transactions monitor the production line andl some others are for higher-level production management. Thus, the performance objectives are to guarantee that all the hard real-time transactions can be completed before their deadlines and then to minimize the number deadline missing of soft real-time transactions.

One of the major problems of the proposed RT-CCPs is that they are not suitable for thie RTDBS with mixed transactions which are different in their criticality (the importance in completing the transactions before their deadlines). They cannot guarantee the schedulability of hard real-time transactions. Although schedulability can be guaranteed by using PCP, it is not suitable for the RTDBS with soft and firm real-time transactions due to its tight assumptions [9].

A single strategy for concumrrency control is not sufficient for RTDBS with mixed transactions. Different conflict resolution strategies have to be used for resolving data conflicts between different types of transactions as the importance of completing them is different. In this paper, we have proposed a new protocol, called Reduce Ceiling Priority (RCP) which is an integration of the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) and the optimistic concurrency control (OCC). The remaining parts of the paper are organized as follows. Section 2 defines the transaction model and introduces an example of RTDBS with mixed transactions. Section 3 defines the proposed Reduced Ceiling Priority (RCP) protocol. Section 4 discusses the characteristics of the proposed protocol.
Section 5 reports the performance of the proposed protocol as compared with OCC-BC. The Conclusions of the paper are in Section 6.

div.head: Transaction Model and Example
div.p: Let the real-time transactions in a RTDBS are classified as hard real-time and sop real-time transactions. Each transaction is deifined with a deadline and a priority. Any violation of the timing constraints of hard real-time transactions may result in a catastrophe.
Missing the timing constraints of soft real-time transactions will only result in the degradation of system performance.

The priority of a soft real-time i.ransaction is defined as a function of its deadline and criticality. The priority of a hard real-time transaction is defined explicitly by application engineers based on the (characteristics of the transactions such as their period of generation. Hard real-time transactions are assigned to higher priorities. No soft real-time transaction has a priority higher than the priority of any hard real-time transaction, Since hard real-time transactions are highly critical, it is assumed that we have more information about the characteristics of the hard real-time transactions. It is supposed that all the hard real-time transactions are periodic and have their timing constraints (their deadlines), read sets, and write sets known before their arrivals, where the read set and the write set of a transaction are the set of data items which may be read and written by the transaction, respectively.

Although the timing constraints (deadlines) of soft real-time transactions are known upon their arrivals, there is no way to know which data items a soft real-time transaction may access until the corresponding operation occurs.
Each transaction (both hard and soft) is defined as a sequence of operations. The processing of an operation requires the access of one or more data items in the database.

Example: An example of RTDBS with mixed transactions is the battlefield management system, which consists of a collection of nodes distributed in different areas. In each node, different types of transactions will be created for different monitoring purposes. One type of the transactions is to detect threats. An example of the threats is the missiles from the enemy. The transactions are periodic hard real-time transactions with known execution time and data requirements. In addition to the periodic hard real-time transactions, other transactions are for the management of the battlefield such as the communications between different nodes and the query transactions on the number of weapons at a node. They are less critical. It is difficult to predict their required data items and execution time, and their arrival times before their arrivals. Different types of the transactions (both soft and hard) share the same database which maintains the information about the current situation of the battlefield and the number of weapons at each node.

3 The Reduced Ceiling Protocol (RCP) We are interested in the context of priority-driven preemptive scheduling. The goal of the Reduced Ceiling Protocol (RCP) is to guarantee the schedulability of hard real-time transactions, and then, to minimize the number of deadline missing of soft real-time transactions. In the RCP, different concurrency control strategies are used to resolve the &iia conflicts between different combinations of hard and soft real-time transactions. The schedulability of hard real-time transactions is ensured by reserving data item for them based on the principles used in the PCP.

The blocking time of a hard real-time transaction is minimized by giving it preferences in using the CPU and the data items over the soft real-time transactions, In order to reduce the number of deadline missing of the soft real-time transactions, the hard real-time transactions are required to release all their seized locks as soon as possible when they no longer need them.

The conflict resolution strategy amongst the soft realtime transactions is following the optimistic approach. The principles used in the RCP in resolving data conflicts can be summarized in Table 1 : In the following sections, we shall descrihe the concurrency control strategies for resolving data mflicts between different combinations of hard and soft real-time transactions.

div.head: Concurrency Control of Hard Real-time Transactions
div.p: In the RCP, lock conflicts among hard real-time transactions are resolved using the strategy similar to the PCP. Each data item is associated with a lock with a ceiling priori9, where the ceiling priority of a lock is defined to be the highest priority of the hard real-time transaction which may access the lock. Before a hard realtime transaction accesses a data item, it has to acquire the lock corresponding to the data item. The lock request of a hard real-time transaction will be denied, i.e., blocked, if the priority of the transaction is not higher than the ceiling priority of all the locks being held by any other hard realtime transactions.

In order to maintain serializability, transactions are required to access data items in a two phase locking (2PL) fashion, i.e., no transaction may request any new lock after it releases any obtained lock. In order to reduce the blocking times of other transaction, a hard real-time transaction will release their seized locks when it will no longer access the corresponding data items.

Note that the locking of any data item from a soft real-time transaction will not block any hard real-time transaction because the definition of the ceiling priority is not affected by the locking from a soft real-time transaction.

div.head: Concurrency Control of Soft Real-time Transactions
div.p: Lock conflicts among soft real-time transactions is resolved by the optimistic approach. The reason is to increase the number of fruitful restarts. Since it is possible that a soft real-time transaction may later be restarted by a hard real-time transaction due to data conflict, it is better to resolve the data conflicts among the soft real-time transactions when one of the soft real-time transactions wants to commit.

In the optimistic approach, the execution of a soft real-time transaction is divided into three phases: (1) the read phase, (2) the validation phase, and (3) the write phase. During the read phase, a soft real-time transaction reads data items from the database but writes data items into its private work space, where a delay write procedure is adopted. A soft real-time transaction locks data items as required, but any lock conflict among soft real-time transactions is ignored. That is, two soft real-time transactions may lock the same data item in a conflicting mode. The conflict is resolved until one of the conflicting transactions enters the validation phase.

During the validation phase, serializability is checked against all the executing transactions with the validating transaction. If there is any data conflict between the validating soft real-time transaction and any executing soft real-time transaction, the later soft real-time transaction is restarted immediately. Different priority conflict resolution methods for the real-time optimistic concurrency control protocols2 [4] can be used to resolve the lock conflicts among soft real-time transactions. However, in here we assume that the validating soft realtime transaction always has an advantage over other executing soft real-time transactions. The favoring of the validating soft real-time transaction is to make the validation process simple and also to comply with the basic assumption of the optimistic protocols in which little conflicting between executing transactions is possible.

Once a soft real-time transaction passes its validation phase, it enters the write phase, and the actual writes of data items in the read phase take effect on the database. Since a soft real-time transaction is near completion when it is at the write phase, it is executing at the highest priority (even higher than the hard real-time transactions) so that it will release its seized locks earlier. This will introduce priority inversion as a hard real-time transaction may be blocked by a soft real-time transaction which is at the write phase. However, as shown in Section 4 below, only one soft real-time transaction will be in the write phase at each time and the maximum number of blocking of a hard real-time transaction is limited to one soft realtime transaction.

No checking of the ceiling priority is needed for any lock requests of soft real-time transactions, and the locking of data item by a soft real-time transaction will not affect the system ceiling (or the ceiling priority of the data item). Soft real-time transactions release their obtained locks when they commit or are aborted.
Other proposed conflict resolution methods are wait-50, sacrifice and any-high [4].

div.head: Concurrency Control between Hard and Soft Real-time Transactions
div.p: In the RCP, hard real-time transactions are given preferences in using the data i t e m as they are more critical. When a soft real-time transaction requests a lock which is already locked by a hard real-time transaction in a non-conflicting mode, it is granted, and the system ceiling is not affected. If the data item is locked by a hard real-time transaction in a conflicting mode, the request is blocked until the hard real-time transaction releases the lock. The reason is that even if the soft real-time transaction is allowed to continue its execution, it is likely that it cannot pass its validation test and will be restarted when either the conflicting hard real-time transaction or itself want to commit.

When a hard real-time transaction requests a lock on a data item which is already locked by a soft real-time transaction, the lock request is granted, and the system ceiling is set as defined in PCP, regardless of whether the data item is locked in a conflicting mode. However, the execution of the soft real-time transaction will not be affected at this time. The checking of any violation of serializability between the hard and soft real-time transactions is done at the validation phase of soft realtime transactions or when the hard real-time transaction wants to commit. When a validlating soft real-time transaction finds that there is any possible violation of the serializability order between the validating soft real-time transaction and any executing hard real-time transaction, the validating soft real-time transaction will be restarted immediately. When a hard real-time transaction wants to commit, it will check what are its conflicting soft realtime transactions. It will restart all the soft real-time transactions which have a readlwrite conflict with it. Those transactions, which have only write/write conflicts, will be allowed to continue. The reason is that since the soft real-time transactions use a delily write principle for the write operations, their serialization order in a serialization graph will be after the hard real-time transactions if the hard real-time transactions commit first.

div.head: Properties of the RCP
div.p: properties of the RCP protocol.

The section is meant to show some important Theorem 1 All the RCP schedules are serializable. Proof. The correctness of this proof directly follows from the facts: (1) The serializability orcler among hard realtime transactions is guaranteed by the two phase locking mechanism. (2) The serializability order between hard real-time transactions and soft real-time transactions is maintained by restarting or blocking of soft real-time transactions if they have data conflicits with hard real-time transactions. (3) The serializability order among soft real-time transactions is maintained at the validation time of soft real-time transactions. When a soft real-time transaction enters the validation phase, all conflicting soft real-time transactions have to be restarted in order to maintain the schedule to be serializable. When a hard real-time transaction wants to commit, it will restart all other conflicting soft real-time transactions if they are in front of it in the serialization order [3] such as due to readlwrite conflict and the read operation from the soft real-time transaction is performed first. Q.E.D.

Lemma 1 There can be only one soft real-time transaction executing in its write phase at any time. Proof. Since soft real-time transactions have lower priority than hard real-time transactions except in their write phase, a soft real-time transaction is not possible to execute and enter its write phase unless no hard real-time transaction is active. Also, when a soft real-time transaction enters its write phase, it runs at the highest priority in the system and will not suffer from any preemption from hard or soft real-time transactions. Therefore, there can be only one soft real-time transaction executing in its write phase at any time. Q.E.D.

Lemma 2 At most one write phase of a soft real-time transaction may block the execution of one request of a hard real-time transaction. Proof. Lemma 1 shows that there can be only one soft real-time transaction executing in its write phase at any time. Also, when the soft real-time transaction leaves its write phase, active hard real-time transactions will start executing and will not suffer from any further blocking from soft real-time transactions. Q.E.D.

Theorem 2 RCP is deadlock-free. Proof. Since PCP and optimistic concurrency control do not generate deadlocks, only deadlocks involving hard and soft real-time transactions may exist under RCP. Also, the only chance that a soft real-time transaction may block a hard real-time transaction is in its write phase. Since a soft real-time transaction running in its write phase does not need to request any more data objects, there should not exist any circular waiting chain for a deadlock which includes hard and soft real-time transactions at the same time. In other words, RCP is deadlock-free. Q.E.D.

div.head: Lemma 3
div.p: The maximum number of priority inversion per request of a hard real-time transaction under RCP is one. Proof. Lemma 2 shows that each request of a hard realtime transaction may experience at most one time of "priority inversion" from soft real-time transactions because of their execution in the write phase. Furthermore. since hard real-time transactions are scheduled by PCP, the maximum number of priority inversion from hard real-time transactions per request of a hard real-time transaction is equal to one according to the properties of PCP. We claim that no request of a hard real-time transaction should experience one priority inversion from some hard real-time transaction and also one priority inversion from some soft real-time transaction. The correctness of the claim comes from the following observation: The reason that a request of a hard real-time transaction may block a request of another hard real-time transaction is because the former arrives at the system earlier than the later. If a request of a soft realtime transaction also blocks the later hard real-time transaction request, the soft real-time transaction request must enter its write phase before the later hard real-time transaction request arrives at the system. In fact, the soft real-time transaction request must also enter its write phase before the former hard real-time transaction request arrives at the system (Please see the proof of Lemma 1). In other words, the soft real-time transaction request should block the former hard real-time transaction request instead of the later. A contradiction exists. Q.E.D.

div.head: Real-time Database Model
div.p: The RTDBS model consists of six components. They are the transaction generators, the scheduler, the CPU, the ready queue, the block queue and the database as shown in Figure 1.

There are two types of transaction generators. One of the generations is responsible for the generation of the soft real-time transactions. The generation is following the Poisson distribution. The other generators generate the hard real-time transactions following their own periods.

Each generated transaction (both hard and soft) will be assigned with a deadline and a priority. The hard realtime transactions have higher priorities than the soft realtime transactions except when the soft real-time transactions are in their write phases. When they are in the write phase, hard real-time transactions are not allowed to preempt them from using the CPU.
The priorities of the hard real-time transactions are defined according to the rate monotonic algorithm [6].

The transaction comes from a shorter period generation will be assigned to a higher priority. For the soft real-time transactions, a higher priority will be assigned to the transaction with a closer deadline.

A transaction is defined as a sequence of operations, either read or write. The probability of an operation to be a write operation is defined to be the read/write ratio (W Ratio). The processing of the operations of a transaction (both soft and hard) requires the use of the CPU and the access of data items in the database. It IS assumed that each operation requires the access of a data item.

div.head: Generators
div.p: Figure 1 : The RTDBS Model The scheduling of the CPU is performed by the scheduler. The transactions are queued in the ready queue for the CPU. At any time, the transaction that has the highest priority gets to use the CPU, unless it is being blocked by other transactions due to lock conflict. It is assumed that the usefulness of completing the soft realtime transactions after their deadlines are zero, they will be aborted once they have missed their deadlines. Before a transaction is allowed to use the CPU, its deadline will be checked. If it has been missed, the transaction will be aborted immediately. If the deadline of a transaction has missed, the transaction will be aborted immediately. Waiting but ready transactions are queued in the ready queue according to their priorities. Since main memory database systems can better support real-time applications, it is assume that the databases are resided in the main memory.

The scheduler is also responsible for managing the locks. Before a transaction accesses a data item, it has to set the lock associated with the data item in the appropriate mode. Based on adopted concurrency control protocol, the scheduler determines whether the lock requesting transaction can be processed, or be blocked in the block queue, or be restarted. If a transaction has to be restarted, all its seized locks have to be released and it has to be restarted from its beginning. After the completion of the commitment procedure, the trarisaction will release all its seized locks and commit.

div.head: Simulation Experiments
div.p: Two simulation models of the above RTDBS model have been implemented using the ,simulation tool OpNet [7] which is a proprietary simulation package. One of the simulation model is using the RCP for concurrency control while the other is wing OCC-BC. The performance of OCC-BC has been shown to be better than HP-2PL for single type RTDBS, under a system with mixed transactions. In the modell with OCC-BC, the execution of the hard real-time transactions will follow the same way as the soft real-time transactions. They have gone through three phases: execution phase, validation phase and write phase. Whenever a validating soft realtime transaction finds that it has ai conflict with a hard real-time transaction, the soft real-time transactions will be restarted. Similarly, all the tramsactions, which are conflicting with a validating hard real-time transactions, will be restarted. Since the validaticin of a transaction has to be performed in a critical section, a hard real-time transaction may be blocked by a soft real-time transaction which is in the validation phase.

The primary performance measure to be used is the miss rate which is defined as the number of deadline missing transactions over the total number of transaction generated. Since there are two types of transactions in the system, two miss rates are defined. They are MRH (miss rate of the hard real-time transactions) and MRs (miss rate of the soft real-time transactions). Since missing the deadline of a hard real-time transaction can be catastrophic, the value of MRH should be zero.

In the simulation model, we have defined five hard real-time generators. Each generator has its own period for the generation of hard real-tirne transactions. The deadline of a hard real-time transaction is defined to be the generation time of the next hard real-time transaction from the same generator.

The deadlines of the soft real-itime transactions are defined based on the expected execution time of the transactions such as: where slack number is a random variable uniformly distributed between the slack bound.

div.head: Simulation Results
div.p: Figure 2 and Figure 3 depict the miss rates, MRs and MRH respectively, under different workload of the soft real-time transactions (different MAR). Although MRs is higher under the RCP than under the OCC-BC when MAR is low, the performance of both the soft and hard real-time transactions are much better under the RCP than under OCC-BC when MAR is high. Higher MSs under OCC-BC is due to greater number of transaction restarts. Under OCC-BC, all data conflicts are resolved by transaction restarts. Increasing the arrival rate of the soft real-time transactions increases the restart probability and thus increases the miss rate. Furthermore, the conflicts are checked only when one of the conflicting transactions enters the validation phase. The cost in restarting a transaction can be very high.

An important observation from Figure 3 is that when the MAR is high, MRH is greater than zero under the OCC-BC. This is highly undesirable. On the contrary, all the hard real-time transactions are guaranteed under the RCP. Fipure 4 and Figure 5 show the miss rates when the worklud of the hard real-time transaction is double (15%) by reducing the periods of the hard real-time transaction generators. Similar to the result in Figure 2 and Figure 3, the performance under the RCP is better than under OCC-BC. MRs increases with an increase in hard real-time transaction workload. The performance under the RCP is better than under the OCC-BC when MAR is high Although MRH is higher under OCC-BC as compared with Figure 3 due to higher hard real-time transaction workload, MRH under the RCP maintains to be zero.

div.head: I Value Number of Hard Real-time Transaction I 5 6 Conclusions
div.p: Although in recent years the research on the design of concurrency control protocols for real-time database systems (RTDBS) has received tremendous interest, most of the proposed protocols are for RTDBS with single type of transactions. If we examine the properties of realistic real-time database applications, we will find that there is a trend of the real-time applications to integrate with other systems. It becomes more common to l w e RTDBS supporting mixed transactions. Different kinds of transactions will have different properties, system requirements and importance of completing them before their deadlines. We call them as RTDBS with mixed transactions. Their performance objectives are to ensure that all hard real-time transactions can be completpd their deadlines and the deadline missing of soft r(-&time transactions can be minimized.

In this paper, we have proposed a new concurrency control protocol, called Reduced Ceiling Priority (RCP) for RTDBS with mixed transactions. In the RCP, different strategies are adopted for resolving the data conflicts between different types of transactions. We have shown the characteristics of the RCP. Simulation experiments have been performed to compare the performance of the RCP with OCC-BC in a RTDBS with mixed transactions. We have found that the RCP not only can guarantee the performance of the hard real-time transactions, at the same time, it can reduce the number of deadline missing of the soft real-time transactions if probability of data conflict is high.
